memory_update.text: Energy theme should be treated as a power-availability and power-delivery chokepoint, not only as oil/gas/uranium/renewables commodity exposure.

Dry-type transformers, power-quality equipment, and magnetics are high-priority underfollowed discovery nodes for AI data centers, industrial electrification, renewables, microgrids, utilities, and semiconductor facilities.

Transmission-line hardware and fittings may offer earlier-order-cycle exposure to grid buildout than EPC contractors, especially where labor-saving installation or utility qualification creates switching costs.

HVDC reactors and high-voltage power-quality components are promising global underfollowed nodes because qualification cycles, reliability standards, and limited supplier bases may create bottlenecks.
Transformer component suppliers such as CTC magnet wire, bushings, tap changers, cores, and insulation should be tracked as speculative second-order beneficiaries of transformer scarcity.
Nuclear fuel-cycle exposure should be separated into mining, conversion, enrichment, HALEU, fabrication, and nuclear-grade components rather than treating all uranium/nuclear equities as one node.

Need Layer 1B searches using filings and primary sources to validate candidate universes for HPS.A, PLPC, Quality Power Electrical Equipments, Končar, nuclear fuel-cycle names, and grid-services specialists.

Oil/gas second-order electrification and reliability nodes remain underdeveloped and should be decomposed in a later pass into LNG power systems, pipeline compression, gas turbine services, field electrification, and methane monitoring.

layer1a.summary: The Energy theme should be decomposed less as a commodity-price trade and more as a multi-decade power-delivery chokepoint: AI/data-center load growth, industrial electrification, renewable interconnection, grid aging, nuclear life-extension/SMR optionality, and oil/gas reliability all converge on scarce electrical equipment, transmission hardware, qualified grid suppliers, nuclear fuel-cycle capacity, and specialized engineering/construction labor. Layer 1A should prioritize bottleneck nodes where demand is broad, qualification cycles are long, suppliers are few, and public-market exposure may sit in obscure small/mid-cap suppliers rather than obvious utilities, hyperscalers, or mega-cap electrical OEMs.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: Transformer and switchgear shortages create a schedule-critical chokepoint for AI/data-center and electrification buildouts. Smaller suppliers with qualified North American or regional manufacturing capacity may benefit before the market fully prices the scarcity.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Prioritize USD 300M-10B or local-market equivalents; include larger diversified names only as reference comps; flag micro-caps as speculative unless backlog, margins, and customer concentration are verifiable.

supply_chain_nodes.why_it_matters: Data centers, factories, renewables, microgrids, EV charging, and utilities all require reliable power conversion, conditioning, and distribution. These components are not as visible as GPUs, turbines, or utilities, but project schedules can be delayed if electrical distribution equipment is unavailable.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: If transmission construction accelerates, specialized hardware suppliers may see orders earlier than EPC revenue recognition. The bottleneck is not only capital spending but also product availability, utility approval, and labor-saving installation methods.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Best hunting zone is small/mid-cap industrials; compare pure-play exposure versus diversified utility-products businesses like Hubbell.

theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Run a two-lane funnel. Use reference leaders such as Vertiv, Eaton, GE Vernova, Quanta Services, Constellation Energy, Cameco, Centrus, BWX Technologies, and hyperscalers only to map the demand signal and validate capex direction. The alpha-discovery lane should search for small/mid-cap or non-US listed suppliers in transformers, dry-type transformers, power quality equipment, transmission-line hardware, HVDC reactors, bushings, magnet wire, nuclear services/fuel-cycle components, testing/inspection, grid construction specialty contractors, and second-order suppliers to Quanta, Siemens Energy, Hitachi Energy, GE Vernova, ABB, utilities, and data-center builders.
supply_side_constraints: Transformer and switchgear lead times, limited factory capacity, and qualified supplier shortages
Transmission permitting delays plus lineworker and construction labor shortages
Long utility and industrial qualification cycles for HV/HVDC components, reactors, transformers, connectors, and protection hardware
Limited nuclear fuel-cycle capacity, especially conversion, enrichment, and HALEU-related capabilities
Specialized EPC, nuclear-grade manufacturing, and quality-assurance bottlenecks
Supplier-risk becoming structural rather than episodic across energy operations
